title: What Is the Trinity? One God in Three Persons
subtitle: The biblical data, the four centuries the church spent working it out, and the one live debate that remains.
triageNote: This is not a hill among hills. This is the ground. The doctrine of the Trinity is the church's confession of who God is. To deny it is to worship a different God than the one Jesus revealed. Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381 did not invent the doctrine. They built a fence around it after a long century of trying to hold the biblical data together without breaking it. So the existence of the triune God, three persons sharing one undivided being, is first-order. The faith itself. There is one genuine in-house debate that runs lower. The page marks it where it comes: whether the eternal relations of Father and Son include an order of authority. That argument is real. It is recent. It runs between people who all confess the Nicene Creed. Hold the doctrine with your life. Hold that one sub-question with care.
question:
The first Christians were Jews who would have died before calling anyone but the Lord their God. The Shema was the daily prayer pressed into them from childhood. Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. They did not abandon that confession. They never thought of themselves as having left it. And then these same hardened monotheists prayed to Jesus. They baptized in his name. They called him Lord in the sense the Old Testament reserved for the unspeakable Name, the kyrios who is the God of Israel. They sang to him as to a god, a Roman governor noticed by the early second century. They spoke of the Spirit as God too, the Spirit who searches the deep things of God and whom no creature could search. And yet they did not think they had three Gods. They did not think Father, Son, and Spirit were three masks one actor wears in turn. So what had they seen. What was forced on them by the resurrection and by the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost that made faithful Jews speak this way without believing they had broken the first commandment.

That is the question this doctrine answers. How can the God who is one be Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each fully God, each truly distinct from the others. Without three Gods. Without dissolving the three back into one. The early church did not reach the answer quickly or cleanly. It took almost three hundred years, from the apostolic writings through the Council of Nicaea in 325 and the Council of Constantinople in 381, with bitter conflict, imperial interference, and exiles in between. Tertullian had already given the Latin West the language of one substance and three persons around the year 200. The East worked toward its own grammar through Origen, through the long crisis Arius set off, through Athanasius and then the Cappadocians. The point was never to produce a riddle that clever people could solve. The point was to confess rightly what God had revealed and to guard that confession against the ways it kept getting broken. The words the church settled on, one being in three persons, eternally begotten, of one substance, were not speculation. Each was chosen against a specific way of getting God wrong, and each marks the place where an earlier teacher had gone over a cliff.
whyItMatters:
Everything stands on this. Not as a slogan. As a structural fact. If the Son is not fully God, then the man on the cross was a creature, however exalted. And a creature cannot reconcile you to God, because the gap between Creator and creature is exactly the gap that needs to be crossed. Your salvation would be a rumor. Athanasius saw this with terrible clarity in the years he spent fighting Arius and the emperors who backed him, exiled five times across more than forty years. He understood that the whole quarrel over a single Greek letter, homoousios against homoiousios, was not academic vanity. It was a fight over whether the one who died for you was God reaching down to save, or a creature who could only point. If the Spirit who dwells in you is not God, then God has not actually come to live in his people. He has sent a substitute, and the New Testament's deepest promise, that God himself indwells you, is hollow. The Cappadocians made the same argument for the Spirit that Athanasius had made for the Son, and Constantinople in 381 wrote the Spirit's full deity into the creed. The Trinity is not the church's hardest puzzle bolted onto an otherwise simple faith. It is the shape of the gospel. God the Father sends God the Son in the power of God the Spirit to bring you into the life the three have always shared.

It also decides who God is in himself, before you and apart from your need of him. A solitary God, one bare person, is power and will and not much else until there is something outside him to act upon. Love only arrives in such a God when there is finally another to love. That makes love an afterthought and creation a kind of necessity, a thing God needed in order to become what he is. But the God who is Father, Son, and Spirit was love before there was a universe. The three have loved one another from eternity, the Father giving all he is to the Son, the Son returning all he is to the Father, the Spirit the bond and the joy of that giving. Augustine reached for exactly this in his De Trinitate, reading the inner life of God along the lines of lover, beloved, and the love between them. God did not become loving when he made you. He is love, in himself, eternally, as the apostle John says without flinching, God is love. Your being loved is the overflow of a love that did not need you to exist in order to be real. That is not a doctrine you admire from a distance. That is the floor under every word the New Testament says about grace.

And it shapes how you pray, whether you have ever thought about it or not. The woman praying over a diagnosis at her kitchen table is not doing trinitarian theology. But trinitarian theology decides what is actually happening when she prays. You come to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. The pattern is everywhere in Paul, most plainly where he says that through Christ we both have access in one Spirit to the Father. The Christian does not pray into the dark and hope someone is listening. The Christian prays inside a conversation that was going on long before the world began. Carried by the Spirit, who intercedes with groanings too deep for words. Presented by the Son, who ever lives to make intercession. Heard by the Father, who was never reluctant and never needed to be persuaded. Lose the Trinity and prayer collapses into a transaction with a single distant sovereign, a creature petitioning a power. Keep it and prayer becomes what it actually is, a creature drawn up by grace into the life that God has eternally been.

positions.name: Pro-Nicene orthodoxy: equal in being, ordered in relation
positions.inOneLine: Father, Son, and Spirit are one in being and equal in every divine attribute, distinguished only by their eternal relations of origin. Nothing else divides them. The order among them is an order of relation, not of authority.
positions.bestCase:
Let me give you the doctrine the church actually settled on. Everything else on this page is a footnote to it. There is one God. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each that one God, fully and without remainder. They share one indivisible divine being. They are not three parts of God, as though deity could be cut into thirds. They are not three Gods standing side by side. The word the Council of Nicaea chose in 325, homoousios, of the same substance, was chosen against a presbyter of Alexandria named Arius. He taught, in a slogan his followers chanted, that there was once when the Son was not. The Son for Arius was the first and highest of all creatures, made by God before time and the agent of all other making, but still on the creature side of the line. The whole council hinged on a single Greek letter, an iota, whether the Son is homoousios, of the same being as the Father, or homoiousios, of a merely similar being. That iota was not pedantry. Athanasius, who came to Nicaea as a young deacon and spent the rest of his life defending its word, was driven from his see five times by emperors who found the compromise parties easier to manage. He saw what was at stake. A Son who is only similar to God is not God. And a savior who is not God cannot save, because only God can bridge the distance between God and us.

Now, how are the three distinct if they share one undivided being. Not by differing in essence, for there is only one essence. Not by dividing the divine attributes among them, for each possesses every one of them wholly. They are distinguished only by their relations of origin. The Father is unbegotten, from no one. The Son is eternally begotten of the Father, light from light, as the creed says, and the creed is careful to add begotten, not made, precisely so that you will not smuggle in a beginning. The Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father. These eternal processions, generation and procession, are the only difference among the persons, and they are differences of relation, not of degree. The Cappadocian fathers, Basil of Caesarea and the two Gregories, of Nazianzus and of Nyssa, gave the East the grammar that finally held in 381 at Constantinople: one ousia, one being, in three hypostases, three persons. Augustine in the Latin West reached the same confession by his own road in De Trinitate, insisting that whatever is said of God as God is said equally of all three. Everything the three do toward the world they do together, because they are one God. The works of the Trinity toward the outside are undivided, a rule the whole tradition kept. Yet each acts in the manner of his relation. The Father as source. The Son as the one through whom. The Spirit as the one in whom.

Is there an order, a taxis, among the persons. Yes, and the tradition has always said so plainly. The Father is the unoriginate source, the fountainhead of deity, the one from whom the Son is begotten and the Spirit proceeds. But hear carefully what kind of order this is. It is an order of origin and relation, not of rank or command. The Son is begotten of the Father, so the Father is first in order of origin. But the Son is in no way less in being, less in glory, less in power, less in authority. To be eternally from another is not to be eternally under another. The Athanasian Creed will not let us blur this: in this Trinity none is before or after, none is greater or less, but the whole three persons are coeternal together and coequal. So when Scripture shows the Son obeying the Father, sent by the Father, doing the Father's will, doing nothing of his own accord, I read all of it as the Son's mission in the world. His taking flesh to save us. What the tradition calls the economy of redemption, distinguished from the eternal life of God as he is in himself. The Son obeys in his humanity, in the days of his flesh, because he has come to do for us what we could not do. The great rule, common to Augustine and the Cappadocians, is that the texts which show the Son as less refer to the form of a servant he assumed, not the form of God in which he eternally subsists. Pull that obedience back into eternity. Make the Son eternally subordinate in authority to the Father. And you have quietly let Arius back in through the side door, because a person eternally under another's authority is not equal in deity, whatever your mouth professes. Authority belongs to the one undivided nature, not to one person over another.

This is the faith of Nicaea and Constantinople, the faith confessed by the whole church, East and West, for sixteen centuries, the faith Bavinck and the Reformed dogmaticians received and handed on. Guard it at the center and you will not go far wrong at the edges.
advocates: the Cappadocian fathers (Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa)
the framers of the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed
modern pro-Nicene retrieval (Lewis Ayres, Khaled Anatolios)

positions.name: Eternal functional subordination of the Son
positions.inOneLine: The Son is fully and equally God in his being. Yet from eternity, not only in the incarnation, he relates to the Father in a role of glad submission. That difference of authority and role does not touch his equality of essence.
positions.bestCase:
Let me be clear about what I am not saying, because I am routinely misheard and even called a heretic for it. I am not Arius. I affirm with my whole heart that the Son is homoousios, of one being with the Father, fully God, eternal, uncreated, equal in every divine attribute and worthy of all worship. I sign the Nicene Creed and the Definition of Chalcedon without crossing my fingers, and I confess the eternal generation of the Son. What I am asking is a narrower question, and I think a fair one. Within that perfect equality of being, is there an eternal order of relationship in which the Son gladly submits to the Father. An order of authority and role, not merely of origin. I say there is, and that this does not touch the Son's equality of essence by the breadth of a hair.

I think Scripture shows exactly this, and shows it reaching beyond the incarnation. The Son is sent by the Father, and never the reverse. Sending implies a real authority in the one who sends, and the Gospel of John presses the Son's being sent again and again. The Father is the head of Christ, Paul says in First Corinthians eleven, in the same breath in which he names Christ the head of man and the man the head of the woman. Headship in Paul is a relation of authority that takes nothing from the worth of the one under it. Look, too, at how the New Testament names the persons. Always Father and Son, in that order, never reversed. The names themselves carry a relation, and a son who eternally submits to a father is honoring him, not confessing himself inferior in nature. And then there is the end of all things, in First Corinthians fifteen. After the resurrection. After the kingdom is handed over. When there is no more curse and no more incarnate work left to finish. Even then, Paul says, the Son himself will be subjected to the one who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all. If the Son's submission were only a temporary arrangement for the days of his flesh, why does it appear at the very consummation, when the flesh has already done its saving work. I take that as a window onto an order that was always there and always will be.

Why does this matter to me, and not as theological hair-splitting. Because it shows that authority and glad submission are not the unhappy results of the fall, invented at Eden to manage sinners. They are written into the eternal life of God himself, in the most beautiful possible form. A Son who delights to do the will of a Father who loves him perfectly and holds nothing back from him. Submission, in God, is not humiliation. It is glory. The Son's eternal yes to the Father is the pattern after which every glad submission in the creation that images God is made. I hold this, with Wayne Grudem and Bruce Ware, precisely to honor the Son, whose obedience the Father crowns with the name above every name. And to ground the goodness of order in the very being of God rather than in the wreckage of the fall.

I know the danger my friends across the table warn of, and I take it seriously. They say an eternal subordination of authority cannot finally be kept apart from a subordination of being, that authority tracks nature, that I am letting Arius in by the back door. I deny it. A human son under his father's authority for a season is fully and equally human, no less a man than his father. Authority and equality of nature are simply not the same axis, and we know this from ordinary life. I grant freely that the burden is on me to keep them apart, and I labor to keep them apart, because I will not surrender one inch of the Son's full and equal deity. But I will not flatten the eternal relations of Father and Son into a bare order of origin with no lived content. Not when Scripture keeps showing me a Son who, being in the very form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself and became obedient. That obedience has roots, and the roots run into eternity.
advocates: much of recent complementarian evangelical theology

positions.name: Pro-Nicene equality against eternal subordination
positions.inOneLine: The Son's obedience belongs wholly to his incarnate mission, the economy of salvation. Reading an eternal hierarchy of authority back into the immanent life of God divides what cannot be divided. It threatens the Son's full deity.
positions.bestCase:
I share everything my brother across the table affirms about the Son's full deity. We are not arguing about whether the Son is God. We are arguing about whether there is an eternal hierarchy of authority inside the one God. And here I have to say, as gently as I can, that the church spent four centuries learning to say no to exactly this, from Nicaea in 325 through Constantinople in 381 and on into Augustine's De Trinitate. I think it was right, and I think the recent recovery of that judgment by writers like Kevin Giles, Fred Sanders, and Thomas McCall is one of the healthier things to happen in evangelical theology in a generation.

Start with what the persons share. There is one divine being, one will, one power, one authority, because there is one God. This is not a stray detail. The church confessed at the Sixth Ecumenical Council in 681 that there are two wills in the incarnate Christ, divine and human, precisely because in his deity he shares the single will of the Godhead. Will and authority are properties of the one divine nature, not possessions of the persons taken separately. The three persons possess that one nature wholly and equally. So to say the Son is eternally under the Father's authority is to say there are two wills within the Godhead, one that commands and one that obeys. That is not Nicene Trinitarianism. That is two beings, however earnestly you protest that you mean one. This is exactly why the tradition located the difference among the persons in the relations of origin alone, begotten and proceeding, and nowhere else. Add authority and submission as a second axis of distinction and you have made the persons differ in something besides relation of origin. The Cappadocians and Augustine forbade that move, because they could see where the road ends. My brother says he is not Arius, and I believe his intent completely and gladly. What I am saying is that the logic of his position, an eternal subordination of authority, cannot in the end be kept from sliding into subordination of being. Authority is not a personal property floating free of nature. It tracks nature. A will that is eternally under command is a lesser will, and a person who has only a lesser will is a lesser God.

What, then, of the sending, the obedience, the Father as head, the Son subjected at the end. I read all of it as the economy, God's saving work in history, and not as a report on the immanent Trinity, God as he is in himself. The Son obeys because he has become man to save us. He is sent because the work of redemption has a shape and an order of mission. His is the role of the one who comes and accomplishes. The great pro-Nicene rule, worked out by Augustine and already present in the Cappadocians, is that texts which show the Son as less than the Father refer to the form of a servant he assumed, not the form of God in which he eternally subsists. Philippians says it in one sentence, holding both forms together: being in the form of God, he took the form of a servant. The obedience belongs to the servant form. As for the head of Christ in First Corinthians eleven, the word kephale can carry the sense of source as readily as ruler, and in any case Paul there names the Father as head of the incarnate Christ, the mediator. And the subjection at the end of First Corinthians fifteen is the incarnate Son presenting the completed kingdom to the Father, the last act of the mediator as man, so that God may be all in all. It is the close of the economy, not a glimpse behind the veil of eternity.

Why do I press this so hard, when we agree the Son is God. Because the equality of the persons is not a side issue. It is the whole achievement of Nicaea, and it took the exile and the blood of confessors to win it. And because the moment you write eternal authority and submission into who God is, you will find people reaching for it to baptize human hierarchies as divinely eternal, which is in fact how this debate reignited among complementarians in the 1990s. The full deity of the Son has been pressed into the service of an argument it was never meant to carry. Keep the Son's obedience where Scripture and the creeds put it, in his mission for us. Then the Son stands exactly as high as the Father, which is to say that no order of command runs through the eternal God at all.
advocates: the historic pro-Nicene consensus (Augustine, the Cappadocians)
much of confessional Reformed and catholic theology

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The deity of the Son, claimed by all orthodox views
biblicalEvidence.summary: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Two claims held together in one sentence: the Word is distinct from God, with God, and the Word is God. John then says all things were made through him. That places the Word on the Creator's side of the line between Creator and creature.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Decisive against Arianism and any view that makes the Son a creature, since what is made through the Word cannot itself be made.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All three positions on this page affirm it fully. The pro-Nicene reading stresses that with God and was God together require both real distinction and full deity. That is the whole grammar of the doctrine. Those who hold eternal functional subordination note that the Word is named in relation, with God, and take that relation to carry an eternal order. Their critics answer that the relation here is one of origin and intimacy, not authority.

biblicalEvidence.summary: I and the Father are one. Spoken in a dispute over whether the Son's works are the Father's works. The crowd takes up stones because they hear a man making himself God. The oneness is strong enough to provoke a charge of blasphemy.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that wants a real gap of rank between Father and Son. The unity here is so close it sounds, to the hearers, like a claim to deity.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Pro-Nicene readers take one as a unity of being and power. Subordinationists note the neuter form, one thing rather than one person. They read it as unity of purpose and work rather than a denial of relational order, while still affirming full deity. Both agree it rules out the Son being a mere creature.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The triune name, claimed by all
biblicalEvidence.summary: Baptizing them in the name, singular, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. One name, three persons. The risen Jesus places the three together as the single object of the church's baptismal allegiance. It is the closest the Gospels come to a formula.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for modalism, which would make the three mere modes, since baptism is into the name of all three as distinct. And hard for tritheism. The name is one.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All orthodox views read this as the seed of the doctrine: one divine name, three distinct persons. The order Father, Son, Spirit is noted by subordinationists as a fixed taxis. Pro-Nicenes answer that an order of naming reflects the relations of origin, the Father as source. It need not imply an order of authority.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Contested between the two readings of order
biblicalEvidence.summary: The Jews sought to kill him because he called God his own Father, making himself equal with God. Then Jesus answers that the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. Equality with God and dependence on the Father, in adjacent verses.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any flat account: verse 18 gives full equality, verse 19 gives the Son doing only what he sees the Father do. The passage refuses to let you drop either.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Eternal functional subordination reads verse 19 as the Son's eternal posture of acting from and after the Father. An order that runs deeper than the incarnation. Pro-Nicene equality reads the Son can do nothing of his own accord as the inseparable operations of the one God. The Son never acts apart from the Father because they are one being. And it reads any subordinate cast as the form of a servant assumed for our salvation. Both insist on verse 18's equality.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God. The relation of God to Christ is set alongside relations of headship. In Paul those carry the sense of authority.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against pro-Nicene equality, since it names God as the head of Christ in a chain of headship relations. It seems to set an order of authority between Father and Son.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Subordinationists take this as authority within equality, the same pattern they see in the Son's eternal relation to the Father. Pro-Nicene readers answer in two ways. First, head, kephale, can carry the sense of source rather than ruler, the head as the spring from which something flows. Second, the Father is here the head of the incarnate Christ, the mediator, the one who took the form of a servant. Not a statement about the eternal Son apart from his mission.

biblicalEvidence.summary: When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all. The Son's subjection appears at the very end, after the kingdom is delivered up.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the view that the Son's subjection is only a temporary feature of the incarnation. It appears at the consummation. And hard for any view that makes the subjection define the Son's eternal being. It is framed as the climax of a saving work that has an end.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Eternal functional subordination reads the Son's subjection at the end as the unveiling of an order that was always there. Pro-Nicene readers take it as the final act of the mediator. The incarnate Son, having completed the kingdom, presents it and himself as man to the Father, so that God is all in all. That is the close of the economy of redemption, not a description of the immanent Trinity. The phrase God may be all in all is read by pro-Nicenes as the goal of redemption. Not the imposition of rank within God.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Pro-Nicene equality, with subordinationists drawing on it
biblicalEvidence.summary: Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. The form of God and the form of a servant are set in deliberate contrast. The obedience to death belongs to the servant form he assumed.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for eternal functional subordination as a reading of the Son's eternal life. It locates the obedience precisely in the form of a servant he took, not in the form of God he eternally had.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Pro-Nicene readers treat this as the master text for the rule that humbling and obedience belong to the assumed servant form, the economy. Equality belongs to the form of God. Subordinationists answer that one who did not grasp at equality but submitted shows a disposition of glad deference. They take that deference to be eternal, not invented at the incarnation, though they grant the deepest humbling is the servant's.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The deity of the Son, claimed by all orthodox views
biblicalEvidence.summary: The Son is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. The Son shares the very nature of God and does the work only God can do, sustaining all things.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Decisive against any subordination of being, since the Son is the exact imprint of God's very nature and upholds creation, a divine work.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All orthodox views affirm it as a high statement of the Son's full deity. Pro-Nicenes note that radiance and imprint language gives distinction without division. The radiance is not less than the light. The verse is common ground. The debate over authority is fought elsewhere, since here only nature and divine work are in view.

weighing:
My judgment, offered as one pastor thinking out loud, not as a verdict you must accept to be orthodox.

First, the thing that is not up for debate. The doctrine of the Trinity itself, one God in three persons, the Son and the Spirit fully and equally God, is the faith. I hold it without hesitation and without the slightest sense that I am holding a private opinion. Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381 were not committees overreaching their warrant. They were the church learning, under enormous pressure and at real cost, to say in stable words what the New Testament had already shown in narrative and prayer. The God of Israel is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Athanasius was right, and the iota he refused to surrender was the difference between a Savior who is God and a savior who is only the highest creature. The exiles he endured, and the long stretch when it seemed the whole empire had gone Arian, are part of why I can write this sentence as settled at all. The Trinity is not negotiable. It is not a puzzle bolted onto an otherwise simple gospel. It is the gospel's own shape, the Father sending the Son in the Spirit to draw us into the life the three have always shared.

Now the one live debate, and here I am genuinely offering an opinion rather than reciting the creed. On whether the Son is eternally subordinate in authority to the Father, I find myself with the pro-Nicene equality reading, and I will tell you why, tentatively, knowing godly people land elsewhere. The decisive point for me is the unity of will. If there is one divine being, there is one divine will, which is why the church confessed against the monothelites that the obeying will in Christ is his human will, not a second will within the Godhead. A Son eternally under the Father's authority seems to require two wills in God, one that commands and one that obeys, and that is a crack the tradition worked very hard to keep out. It located the difference among the persons only in the relations of origin, begotten and proceeding, and it did so precisely so that nothing belonging to the one divine nature, authority included, would be parceled out among them. When I read the obedience texts, the sending in John, the head of Christ is God in First Corinthians eleven, the subjection at the end in First Corinthians fifteen, they read most naturally to me as the economy, the Son's saving mission, the form of a servant he took. Philippians two seems to me to say almost that in as many words, setting the form of God against the form of a servant. And I notice, with some unease about the other view, that an eternal hierarchy inside God is hard to keep from sliding into a hierarchy of being, however firmly its defenders deny that they mean any such thing.

But I want to say several honest things on the other side, because this is a family argument and I owe my brothers fairness. The men who hold eternal functional subordination, Wayne Grudem and Bruce Ware chief among them, are not Arians, and they do not deserve to be called such. They affirm the full and equal deity of the Son as loudly as anyone alive, and they confess the homoousios without reservation. They are reaching for something genuinely true, that the relations of Father and Son are not interchangeable, that order and glad deference can be beautiful rather than degrading, that the names Father and Son carry a real and irreversible relation. And they have real texts on their side, especially the Son's subjection at the very consummation in First Corinthians fifteen, which appears after the incarnate work is finished and is harder for my position than I would prefer to admit. So I land here. The Trinity, first-order, settled, the floor beneath everything. The eternal-authority question, a real debate among the orthodox. I lean firmly pro-Nicene, while insisting that it is an argument inside the family and not a wall between believers.
charitableDisagreement:
Be careful how you fight this one. Two very different things are on the table, and treating them the same does damage in both directions. The doctrine of the Trinity is first-order. Someone who denies that the Son is fully God, who makes him a creature in the manner of Arius or a passing mode of the one person in the manner of Sabellius, has stepped outside the Christian confession and is worshiping a god other than the one Jesus revealed. Clarity there is not unkindness. It is the most basic honesty the church owes the world and owes the inquirer. Arius was not a brother with an interesting alternative to weigh. He was wrong about who God is, and the council that named him wrong was doing its plain duty. There is no false peace to be bought by softening that. The line around the deity of the Son and the Spirit is the line around the gospel itself.

The debate over eternal authority and submission is a different kind of thing entirely, and the temperature of it in recent years has not been to anyone's credit. When it broke into the open among evangelicals, brothers who confess every line of the Nicene Creed found themselves charged with heresy by other brothers who confess the same lines, and the charges flew in both directions. That is a scandal, and it should grieve us. I know the reflex from the inside. The heresy charge feels like courage while you are making it, and it almost never is. If you hold the pro-Nicene equality view, as I lean to, do not call those who hold eternal functional subordination Arians. They are not, they affirm the homoousios without flinching, and the accusation tells more about your zeal than your accuracy. State your worry about the unity of will honestly and let it be weighed, but do not unchurch a brother over it. If you hold eternal functional subordination, do not treat the pro-Nicene insistence on one will and one authority as a cold abstraction invented to win an argument. It does not empty the Father and Son relation of all content. It is the hard-won grammar, paid for at Nicaea and Constantinople, that kept the Son fully God in the first place, and the people pressing it are guarding something they have a duty to guard.

So, is it a hill to die on. The Trinity itself, yes, with everything you have, because to lose it is to lose the God of the gospel and to be left worshiping something smaller. The eternal-authority question, no. It is a debate the church can hold, and ought to hold far better than it has lately, between people who kneel before the same triune God and will go on kneeling before him forever. Defend the doctrine like the ground it is. Conduct the sub-debate like a family argument among people who will spend eternity together in the presence of the very God they are arguing about, which ought to make all of us slower to condemn and quicker to listen.

relatedDebates.topic: The filioque and the procession of the Spirit
relatedDebates.note: The original Constantinopolitan creed says the Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Western church later added and the Son, the filioque. The Eastern church never accepted it, and it remains a central difference between East and West. The question is whether the Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son together. It bears directly on how the three persons are ordered.

relatedDebates.topic: Modalism, Arianism, and the boundaries the creeds drew
relatedDebates.note: The doctrine was hammered out against two opposite errors. Modalism, that Father, Son, and Spirit are three masks of one person, collapses the three. Arianism, that the Son is the highest creature, collapses the deity. Every phrase of the Nicene Creed is aimed at one or the other. That is why the wording matters and cannot be loosened without letting an old error back in.

relatedDebates.topic: The eternal generation of the Son
relatedDebates.note: The creed calls the Son begotten, not made, eternally begotten of the Father. Some recent evangelicals questioned whether eternal generation is biblical or merely a Greek philosophical import. Others have argued strongly for its recovery. Where you stand shapes how you understand what distinguishes the persons at all. The relations of origin are the only difference the tradition allows.
